albums.blurb: Ronnie Foster is a Buffalo-born organist who spent the early seventies as one of Blue Note's house groove-makers before going on to sideman work for George Benson and Stevie Wonder. Two Headed Freap is his debut as a leader, cut at Rudy Van Gelder's studio in January 1972 with a small band of harp, guitar, vibes, bass and drums: five originals plus organ instrumentals of then-current soul hits by Al Green, Wilson Pickett and Joe Simon. Entirely instrumental, it sits squarely in the era's cinematic, greasy organ-funk vein.
albums.reception: AllMusic rates the album four and a half stars, and its original "Mystic Brew" became one of Blue Note's most-recycled grooves after A Tribe Called Quest sampled it for "Electric Relaxation", with later covers by BADBADNOTGOOD and the Vijay Iyer Trio.

albums.blurb: Electric Guest is the Los Angeles duo of falsetto-voiced singer Asa Taccone and drummer Matthew Compton. Mondo, their debut, was produced entirely by Danger Mouse and released on Downtown Records in April 2012, folding Motown-style soul, synth-pop and California slacker rock into ten tight tracks — plus the nine-minute two-part suite "Troubleman". The band followed it with Plural in 2017, the album your liked songs cluster on.
albums.reception: Mondo reached No. 32 on the French albums chart and No. 11 on Billboard's Heatseekers chart, while lead single "This Head I Hold" peaked at No. 30 on Billboard's Alternative Songs chart and ranked among France's year-end best-selling singles of 2012.

albums.blurb: Slowdive formed in Reading, England around the twin voices of Neil Halstead and Rachel Goswell. Souvlaki, their second album for Creation Records, is the band's defining statement: slow-motion guitar haze wrapped around real songs, with Brian Eno contributing to "Sing" and "Here She Comes". It arrived just as Britpop was shoving shoegaze out of fashion in the UK; the band was dropped after their next record and only reunited in 2014.
albums.reception: On release Souvlaki peaked at No. 51 on the UK Albums Chart to largely tepid reviews, but it has since been reappraised with retrospective acclaim as one of the defining classics of shoegaze.
